<p>“The air was saturated with cement dust,” said lifelong Northampton, Pa., resident LeRoy Brobst, 58.</p>
<p>As a child, his chore was to sweep the cement dust from his family’s sidewalk every day.</p>
<p>“Otherwise, if it rained on it, it became part of the sidewalk,” he said.</p><div class="s2nPlayer k-wQoDAMss" data-type="float" data-s2n-api="dfm_stn_player_script_id_wQoDAMss"></div><script>	function dfm_stn_player_script_id_wQoDAMss( getS2NApiForPlayer ) {

			const s2nApi = getS2NApiForPlayer( document.querySelector('.k-wQoDAMss') );

		}
	}</script>

<p>Drawn by geology that created some of the best cement-producing limestone in the world, dozens of cement companies sprang up from Fogelsville to Whitehall to Nazareth to Martin’s Creek.</p>
<p>Though only five local cement plants remain, the industry’s legacy is still visible at the Atlas Cement Memorial Museum–a monument to Northampton’s Atlas Cement, once the world’s largest cement producer.</p>
<p>The museum, located at the Northampton Borough Municipal Building, is marking its 10th season.</p>
<p>“I saw these plants throughout the area dying one by one, from a total of 30 companies to five,” said Edward Pany, a former Atlas employee who founded the museum in 1997.</p>				<div class="dfp-ad dfp-outstream_video" id="div-gpt-ad-outstream_video" style="visibility:hidden">
					<div class="htlad-outstream_video" data-unit='chicagotribune.com/news/outstream_video' data-targeting=''></div>
				</div>
<p>The exhibit, he said, is a way of “preserving our history and heritage … to remember the men and the women who worked at this Atlas plant.”</p>
<p>Family ties in cement making not only go back two or three generations, but to Austria, Hungary, Russia and elsewhere. The museum displays Atlas company manuals written in German and other languages.</p>
<p>Pany’s father, Anthony, came from Austria as a child and worked at “the Atlas” his entire life. Edward Pany also worked there during summers in the 1950s, earning $2.02 per hour.</p>
<p>“I was taught dozens of different jobs in the plant,” he said. Some days, he worked near the 2,700-degree Fahrenheit cement kilns. He spent other days in the deafening grinding area, where stone was ground to powder in giant steel drums.</p>				<div class="dfp-ad dfp-cube_article" id="div-gpt-ad-cube_article" style="visibility:hidden">
					<div class="htlad-cube_article" data-unit='chicagotribune.com/news/cube_article' data-targeting=''></div>
				</div>
<p>“After the first night you came home, you didn’t hear anything,” Pany said, noting that nobody wore ear protection. There also weren’t hard hats, and sometimes not even gloves.</p>
<p>Pany, 70, went on to become a U.S. history teacher at Northampton Area High School for 39 years. Now retired, he also is a borough councilman.</p>
<p>The story of the Lehigh Valley’s cement starts more than 450 million years ago, when much of the East Coast was covered by a shallow ocean, said Helen Delano, a geologic scientist with the Pennsylvania Geological Survey in Middletown, Dauphin County.</p>
<p>Corals, shellfish and other marine animals pulled minerals out of the water to build skeletons and shells, Delano said.</p>
<p>Over millions of years, the crushed shells were compressed into the “Jacksonburg Limestone,” a rock formation stretching from Berks through Northampton counties.</p>
<p>To make cement, Delano said, “you need to mix a lot of limestone and a little bit of clay and some other things” and then heat the mix to change it chemically.</p>
<p>In the Lehigh Valley, builders in the 1800s realized local rock had almost the perfect blend of minerals “right out of the ground,” Delano said.</p>
<p>In 1871, a local entrepreneur named David Saylor “experimented in his kitchen” with stone from Coplay to make an even better product called “Portland cement,” said Martha Capwell Fox, a local historian and co-author of “The Lehigh Valley Cement Industry.”</p>
<p>In the early 1890s, Saylor’s Coplay Cement Co. also built the towering cement kilns now preserved in Saylor Park in Coplay.</p>
<p>Atlas, founded in Coplay in 1889, moved to what would become Northampton in 1895. Before using steam engines, the company owned 200 horses to maintain its farms and haul limestone from its quarry.</p>
<p>The Atlas museum features a papier-mache horse that Atlas harnessmaker Calvin Bartholomew kept in a display window as a kind of mannequin.</p>
<p>The museum’s walls are lined with quotations from the personal histories Pany collected from every Atlas employee he could find. At its height in the early 20th Century, Atlas had 5,000 employees and processed 9,000 tons of rock per day.</p>
<p>One of the museum’s most recent acquisitions are handwritten documents from one of Atlas’ biggest projects: the Panama Canal, built using more than 8 million barrels of Atlas cement.</p>
<p>Today, most of the cement manufacturing process has been automated. And while that means a plant needs only 150 to 200 employees instead of thousands, the automation has helped keep local cement companies profitable, said Stephen Hayden Jr., plant manager at Keystone Cement in East Allen Township.</p>
<p>“For the most part, it’s really the only remaining heavy industry in the Valley,” Hayden said. “Without the onslaught of modern technology … it’s possible that these plants would have gone the way of Bethlehem Steel.”</p>
<p>Coplay Cement was bought out in 1976 by a company later renamed Essroc. In 1980, Atlas was bought by Lehigh Portland Cement–now based in Upper Macungie Township and a subsidiary of the Heidelberg Cement Group.</p>
<p>Atlas’ last plant in Northampton closed in 1982, and its 250-foot smokestack was demolished in 1993.</p>
<p>But the industry’s story doesn’t end there, Pany stressed, pointing to one of his favorite quotations at the museum.</p>
<p>It’s a statement by Pany’s godfather, 92-year-old Frank Wolfer of Whitehall Township, who worked at the plant for more than 45 years:</p>
<p>“The Atlas plants are now sleeping … but the memories of the men and women who worked there will live forever.”</p>
<p>– – –</p>
<p>Cement industry once was dominant</p>
<p>In 1871, David Saylor, founder of Coplay Cement Co., obtained the first American patent for “Portland cement,” a better mix of cement than is found in nature. From about 1905 to the early 1920s, 5,000 employees worked for Atlas Cement, when it was the biggest cement producer in the world.</p>
<p>151,000 barrels of Atlas cement were used to build the Empire State Building.</p>
<p>8 million barrels of Atlas cement were used to construct the Panama Canal.</p>
<p>30 cement companies were running in eastern Pennsylvania at the industry’s height.</p>
<p>5 local cement companies operate today.</p>
<p>The former Atlas Cement plant in Northampton, Pa., closed in 1982.</p>
<p>Sources: Exhibits at the Atlas Cement Memorial Museum, Edward Pany.</p>
<p>— The Morning Call</p>
